title: Overage Drinking: A National Concern

jokes.text: Group watches two young people make out, debating whether it's weird to watch vs. 'it's hot'
jokes.setup: Two people are making out intensely in the bar; the gang debates the ethics of watching
jokes.punchline: The counter-argument to 'it's weird we're watching' is 'it'd be weird if we DIDN'T watch' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny cold open energy — the gang's moral rationalizations are the joke. 'It'd be weird if we didn't watch' is a good inversion of the expected response, characteristic of these characters' twisted logic.

dialogue.line: Characters watching underage kids make out with 'too much tongue' and debating whether it's weird to watch

jokes.text: Teenager calls one of the gang 'grandpa' after being asked if he's 21
jokes.setup: Gang member challenges a young-looking guy about his age
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, fuck off, grandpa' — the reversal where the person being questioned insults the asker's age
jokes.explanation: The 'grandpa' insult lands because it immediately wounds Dennis (who is obsessed with his appearance and youth) and the gang's reaction — 'The mouth on him' — confirms they're stung by it. Economy is high: two words do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Trey Jr.
dialogue.line: Yeah, fuck off, grandpa.

jokes.text: 'Wait a second, didn't we, like, just deal with this?' / 'We just dealt with something like this.'
jokes.setup: The gang is confronting a young couple in the bar, an apparent repeat scenario
jokes.punchline: Both Dennis and Dee acknowledge this is a recurring situation for them, implying their lives are an absurd loop
jokes.explanation: Mildly meta — teasing that the gang keeps ending up in these situations. Works as character comedy and sets up the reveal that these are old acquaintances. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing, you know exactly what's coming.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: This is classic Tammy.

jokes.text: It turns out the kids in the bar are the gang's own children/connections — 'Goddamn it, son.'
jokes.setup: The gang is about to kick out young troublemakers from the bar
jokes.punchline: The troublemaker turns out to be their own kid — the authority figures are exposed as the most ridiculous people in the room
jokes.explanation: Good structural reversal — the gang positioning themselves as moral gatekeepers only to be immediately undermined by their own family mess. 'Goddamn it, son' is a great deflation of their pretense.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Huh? Did you say something? I wasn't listening.

jokes.text: 'That turned into a real Romeo and Juliet thing, didn't it?' followed by genuine confusion about what to do
jokes.setup: A dramatic scene just played out involving young lovers and disapproving parents
jokes.punchline: Dennis romanticizes the cliché while being completely oblivious that he IS one of the disapproving adults in this scenario
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-absorption — narrating the drama as if he's not part of it — is consistent character work. Mild laugh, sets up the episode's theme of teen drama vs. adult drama.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, because I am an adult, and I like adult stories, like a sexual psychological thriller.

jokes.text: 'Oh, shit. This is classic Tammy.'
jokes.setup: The couple introduces themselves as Trey and Tammy — names that apparently mean something to the gang
jokes.punchline: Mac's instant recognition and casual 'classic Tammy' implies a whole world of Tammy lore that the audience doesn't yet have
jokes.explanation: Economy is excellent — three words do enormous comedic work by implying a rich backstory with total confidence. The casualness of 'classic Tammy' is what makes it land. High quotability as a reaction line.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: You were 30.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Okay, well, let's not do that, you know?

jokes.text: Mac delivers an exhaustive, breathless backstory summary of Trey, Tammy, Dennis, Dee, Trey Jr., and Kerry Bitaberry in a single talking-head monologue
jokes.setup: The audience needs context for who Trey and Tammy are
jokes.punchline: The backstory is absurdly convoluted and delivered with zero self-awareness, ending with 'I think they're gonna try to bang them' as the logical conclusion of all this drama
jokes.explanation: Mac's talking-head exposition is a great format joke — the show using its own structure to mock soap opera convolution. The name 'Kerry Bitaberry' is funny on its own. The confident conclusion ('they're gonna try to bang them') perfectly encapsulates the gang's predictability. High character integration because only Mac would deliver this with such earnest authority.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Time's all in your head, Tammy. And in your ass, apparently.

jokes.text: Charlie's rapid-fire exposition monologue explaining the entire Trey-Tammy-Dennis-Dee history in a talking head.
jokes.setup: We cut to Charlie in a confessional delivering what appears to be context for the audience.
jokes.punchline: The exposition becomes increasingly absurd — 'they had a baby named Trey Junior,' 'Trey Junior's in love with Kerry Bitaberry,' 'the Bitaberry family is trash, which they are' — culminating in Charlie immediately repeating all of it to Mac who clearly doesn't care.
jokes.explanation: Charlie as the gossip repository of intricate teen drama lore is a great character bit. The structure — deliver it to camera, then immediately repeat it to someone who explicitly doesn't care — is well-constructed. 'The Bitaberry family is trash, which they are' is delivered with absolute conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You know, sometimes I feel like she might be the one that got away.

jokes.text: 'Dude, I don't give a flying fuck about any of this gossipy bullshit.' / 'Oh, you're not into teen drama?'
jokes.setup: Mac excitedly summarizes the Trey/Tammy backstory to Charlie
jokes.punchline: Charlie's total dismissal — he wasn't even listening — followed by Mac's innocent reframe as 'teen drama'
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie/Mac dynamic. Charlie's 'I wasn't listening' paired with Mac's undeterred cheerfulness is good character work. The 'teen drama' label sets up the episode's central comic argument.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's probably gonna wind up in a rape or a murder.

jokes.text: Charlie prefers 'a sexual psychological thriller' over teen drama — 'No, because I am an adult, and I like adult stories'
jokes.setup: Mac labels their situation 'teen drama'; Charlie objects
jokes.punchline: Charlie, one of the most childlike and least adult characters on TV, insisting he's into sophisticated adult fare — with no self-awareness
jokes.explanation: High character integration — Charlie insisting on 'adult stories' while being demonstrably the least adult person in the room is a perfect Sunny irony. This also sets up the episode's meta-commentary on narrative genres, which is an unusually clever structural device for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You know we can hear you? I would never do that.

jokes.text: 'Well, since we were in high school. You were 30.' / 'Okay, well, let's not do that.' / 'Time's all in your head, Tammy.'
jokes.setup: Dennis says it's hard to believe they haven't seen each other 'since high school'
jokes.punchline: Tammy notes he was 30 when he was in high school with them; Dennis's deflection — 'Time's all in your head' — is both desperate and absurd
jokes.explanation: Dennis's vanity and delusion are his defining traits, and 'Time's all in your head, Tammy' is a great line — it sounds almost philosophical while being completely defensive. The callback to earlier 'you look familiar' pays off with this age joke. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's actually not a cologne. No, that's a pheromone serum. I heard about it on Rogan.

jokes.text: 'And in your ass, apparently.' — Dee's rejoinder about time being 'in your ass'
jokes.setup: Dennis says 'Time's all in your head, Tammy' as a defensive deflection about his age
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately adds '...and in your ass, apparently' — a crude anatomical capper that deflates the pseudo-profundity
jokes.explanation: Quick and efficient crude joke that punctures Dennis's moment of self-delusion. 'That's... she's just making a joke. Yeah, it's true.' from Dennis and Tammy respectively shows it lands in-world too. Economy is high for such a blunt payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's, like, testicular fluid from, like, a bull's prostate or something like that.

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee agree to pick up their kid's bar tab as a legal obligation — 'I actually think that's a law'
jokes.setup: Trey assumes they'll pay their child's bar tab since the kids ran out
jokes.punchline: Dennis fabricates a legal justification rather than simply admitting responsibility, then Dee pressures Dennis to hurry and he gave 'way too much'
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Dennis inventing legal cover for basic social obligations is on-brand. 'You gave him way too much' is a minor beat. Nothing exceptional here but it flows naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Human females?

jokes.text: Dennis nervously explaining: 'That's... she's just making a joke.'
jokes.setup: Tammy makes a crude comment about Dennis's aging anatomy in front of everyone.
jokes.punchline: Dennis awkwardly tries to cover — 'she's just making a joke' — with the transparent insecurity of a man who absolutely took it personally.
jokes.explanation: Good beat that extends the joke. Dennis's vanity makes the defensive scramble feel earned. 'It's true' from someone else twisting the knife would have elevated it further.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Did one of you step in dog shit?

jokes.text: Mac's talking head: 'It's probably gonna wind up in a rape or a murder.'
jokes.setup: Mac is calmly predicting what Dennis and Dee's plan to seduce Trey and Tammy will result in
jokes.punchline: He casually predicts rape or murder as the likely outcome, then immediately adds 'What? Jesus Christ. You know we can hear you?'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Mac's breezy prediction of 'rape or murder' as the logical endpoint of a Dee-and-Dennis scheme is perfectly calibrated dark comedy — it acknowledges the show's history without winking too hard. The structure is excellent: calm prediction → shocked reaction from Dennis ('What?') → 'Don't tell her, though' as the kicker. Economy is superb. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, you know what that is? That's the old piss cans. I haven't changed them in, like, forever.

jokes.text: 'You know we can hear you? I would never do that.' / 'Well... Don't tell her, though.'
jokes.setup: Mac says in a talking head that Dennis and Dee's scheme will 'probably end in rape or murder.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis protests he'd never do that — but then immediately whispers to Mac not to tell Dee, implying the concern is specifically about her.
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke with a great structure. First beat: Dennis's plausible denial. Second beat: the aside to Mac about not telling Dee immediately reveals he's not denying the act itself, just excluding himself — implying Dee would absolutely do it. Perfectly dark, perfectly in-character for both. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Buddy, how... I don't get it. I mean, how can you be so obsessed with cleaning the bar, and yet you live in all this piss and shit?

jokes.text: Dennis explains his pheromone serum is 'testicular fluid from, like, a bull's prostate or something like that' — heard about it on Rogan
jokes.setup: Dee notices an awful smell; Dennis reveals he's wearing a 'pheromone serum'
jokes.punchline: The serum is 'testicular fluid from a bull's prostate' sourced from Joe Rogan's podcast — a perfect convergence of Dennis's vanity, pseudoscience credulity, and social obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The specificity — 'testicular fluid from, like, a bull's prostate OR SOMETHING LIKE THAT' (the casual uncertainty making it worse) — combined with the Rogan source is sharp cultural satire. It's also a great visual gag: Dennis believes he's irresistible and he literally smells like bull testicle. The follow-up 'Human females?' from Dee is the perfect one-word dismantling. High character integration — Dennis's vanity + his susceptibility to bro-science is very specific to him.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, no, come on. Don't be silly. It's just the excuse I made to sort of peel off and be alone with you.

jokes.text: 'Human females?' — Dee's one-word question after Dennis claims the pheromone serum is 'scientifically proven to drive females wild'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims the bull prostate serum drives 'females wild'
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat 'Human females?' implies the obvious absurdity — that this might work on cows but not people
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum impact. It's the perfect Dee line — not sarcastic, genuinely asking, which makes it funnier than if it were a knowing wisecrack. Economy scores 10 because it cannot be shorter. Highly quotable as a standalone reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's your fault, mister, because, uh, you get things moving inside me, you know?

jokes.text: Dennis explains the serum not working on Dee is proof it's working — 'You're my sister, okay? If it was working on you, we'd have a real problem'
jokes.setup: Dee notes the smell isn't doing anything for her, implying the serum doesn't work
jokes.punchline: Dennis reframes this as evidence of the serum's precision — but the logic implies that if it DID work on Dee, incest would be on the table, which he treats as merely inconvenient
jokes.explanation: The incest implication — treated as a mild logistical concern rather than a moral horror — is very Sunny. Dennis's tone of 'That would be bad. All right.' is perfectly calibrated: not denial, just practical concern. Dark and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Trey
dialogue.line: I got to take a shit.

jokes.text: Dennis suggests the smell might be 'a cool spring breeze? Perhaps some, uh, freshly hung laundry?' while Tammy clearly smells something horrible
jokes.setup: Tammy keeps noting the terrible smell at her door; Dennis keeps proposing increasingly absurd innocent explanations
jokes.punchline: The gap between 'freshly hung laundry' and 'dog shit' is the joke — Dennis's reality distortion field in full effect
jokes.explanation: Dennis's escalating alternative explanations for his own stench is a good sustained bit. 'Freshly hung laundry' is a particularly funny attempt — it's so domestic and innocent compared to what he's actually wearing.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I live free. Like a wild beast.

jokes.text: Tammy answers the door, immediately asks 'Did one of you step in dog shit?' because of Dennis's pheromone serum smell
jokes.setup: Dennis has been wearing bull-prostate pheromone serum convinced it's sexually attractive; they've arrived at Tammy's door
jokes.punchline: Tammy's first reaction is to ask if someone stepped in dog shit — his seduction tool smells like feces
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the pheromone serum setup. The escalating smell descriptions — 'fertilized lawn,' 'cool spring breeze,' 'freshly hung laundry,' then 'dog shit' — are a well-structured escalation that builds to the most humiliating possible answer. Dennis's increasingly desperate alternative suggestions make it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Let's bang and make Trey jealous.

jokes.text: Tammy asks them to take their shoes off at the door — silent reaction beat as Dennis realizes his seduction plan is starting with removing his shoes
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee have arrived at Tammy's home with seduction plans; Tammy thinks they stepped in dog shit
jokes.punchline: The polite suburban request to remove shoes completely deflates any seductive tension — 'Jesus... No problem. Don't. Just don't.'
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke — the mundane domesticity of 'take your shoes off' punctures Dennis's self-image as a suave seducer. 'Don't. Just don't.' suggests Dee telling Dennis not to make it weird, which he inevitably will.

dialogue.line: I have to take a shit.

jokes.text: Mac arrives at Charlie's apartment and immediately senses Dennis's presence from the smell: 'Has Dennis been here? I feel both intimidated and aroused.'
jokes.setup: Mac shows up at Charlie's; the pheromone serum was established as meant to intimidate males and attract females
jokes.punchline: Mac — a man — reports feeling both intimidated AND aroused by the residual smell, which raises questions about Mac's sexuality that the show has long teased
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback. The serum was described as intimidating to males and attractive to females — Mac feels BOTH, which is a perfect, economical joke about his long-running sexual identity arc. 'I feel both intimidated and aroused' is an immediately quotable line. The structure is perfect: setup in one scene, payoff three scenes later, and the payoff does double duty (pheromone joke + Mac's sexuality). High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why do they call them that? There's no soap involved. And no singing. Nothing operatic about it.

jokes.text: Charlie attributes the smell to 'the old piss cans. I haven't changed them in, like, forever.'
jokes.setup: Mac senses the pheromone smell and wonders if Dennis was there
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually reveals he has 'piss cans' in his apartment that he hasn't changed, presented as a completely normal explanation
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie detail — the 'piss cans' are horrifying but delivered with complete normalcy. 'I haven't changed them in, like, forever' implies this is a maintenance task rather than a sanitation crisis. Very character-specific: only Charlie lives this way.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: What's good, baby? What's poppin'?

jokes.text: Mac can't understand Charlie's obsession with cleaning the bar while living in 'all this piss and shit' — 'It's both of you' referring to Charlie and Frank
jokes.setup: Mac points out the contradiction between Charlie's bar-cleaning obsession and his squalid apartment
jokes.punchline: 'I mean, how can you be so obsessed with cleaning the bar, and yet you live in all this piss and shit?' — the hypocrisy is the joke, and it's completely true
jokes.explanation: Good character observation that's true to Charlie's established personality — his 'Charlie work' at the bar has always been contrasted with his feral home life. Not a standout joke but solid character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: If this got something to do with that john who got his dick bit off, I don't know shit, all right?

jokes.text: Dee reveals she 'took a shit' as the actual reason for her bathroom break, not just the excuse she made
jokes.setup: Earlier Dee suggested 'take a shit' as an excuse to split off; she's now alone with Trey, suggesting she used this excuse
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, I took a shit. But you know what? That's your fault, mister, because you get things moving inside me' — the crude joke is her using her bowel reaction as a seduction line
jokes.explanation: Great payoff — the 'shit excuse' that Dennis dismissed as 'too gross' turns out to be literally true, and Dee attempts to weaponize it as a flirtatious line ('you get things moving inside me'). The delivery of using digestive disruption as a compliment is peak Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Jack Kelly, attorney at lawyering.

jokes.text: Trey confesses things 'aren't great between me and Tammy, sexually-wise right now' and suggests 'spicing things up in the bedroom'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to seduce Trey; Trey seems receptive to her flirtation
jokes.punchline: He's not suggesting infidelity — he's suggesting Dee help him fix his marriage. 'Maybe spicing things up in the bedroom might help.' He means with Tammy.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirect — Dee thinks she's making progress, but Trey is just asking for marriage advice. The deflation is well-timed and sets up the extended joke of Trey's domestic situation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You have an office? That in itself is a mysterious twist. No, he doesn't. He's talking about my mom's basement.

jokes.text: Revelation that Trey does all the laundry, grocery shopping, dog walking, AND dishes while Tammy makes all the money — 'I've been killing it in fantasy football'
jokes.setup: Trey mentions he needs to finish the laundry; Dee starts asking follow-up questions
jokes.punchline: Each question reveals another domestic chore Trey handles, culminating in 'Tammy makes all the money' and his defense of himself: 'I've been killing it in fantasy football'
jokes.explanation: Well-structured escalation joke — each new domestic task revealed is funnier than the last because Dee's growing disillusionment mirrors the audience's. 'I've been killing it in fantasy football' as a defense of his life choices is excellent: it's the pathetic pride of someone grasping at something. The structure (question → reveal → bigger reveal → final humiliation → fantasy football) is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You know what I mean? I got to find Frank. I got to find out what I'm president of. You know, these are, these are big decisions that are kind of over your head, man.

jokes.text: 'Let's bang and make Trey jealous.' — Dee's direct seduction pitch to Tammy
jokes.setup: Dee has spent the scene building up to some kind of seduction of Tammy, using the language of emotional connection and suburban dissatisfaction
jokes.punchline: The 'move' is just: 'Let's bang and make Trey jealous' — the same exact teen drama scheme from high school, delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to the original Tammy/Trey/Dee dynamic from high school — Dee is literally re-running a 20-year-old play. The directness of 'let's bang and make Trey jealous' after Dee's elaborate emotional setup is a great structural deflation. Economy is high: the phrase does so much work in six words.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was going for that forbidden teen drama thing, you know? I convinced her that Trey Jr. cheated on her, and the only way she could get back at him was to sleep with me.

jokes.text: Dee in a talking head: 'Tammy, Tammy, Tammy. It's so great to be alone, finally.'
jokes.setup: Dee begins her alone-time with Tammy with performative casualness.
jokes.punchline: The 'finally' — she's treating this like the culmination of a long plan, as if Tammy had been a barrier to something, when in fact Dee's entire plan is completely transparent.
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. Dee's transparent seduction attempt read as a plot is mildly funny but doesn't land as a standalone moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The whole thing was done in silence. Except for the noises that I was making.

jokes.text: Tammy's disgusted 'Oh, God. That's what this is about? Yeah. I'm not gonna bang you.'
jokes.setup: Dee pitches 'let's bang and make Trey jealous'
jokes.punchline: Tammy's flat refusal — not shocked, just tired — implies this is somehow a recognizable pattern
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat — Tammy's weary 'I'm not gonna bang you' rather than outrage suggests she half-expected this. The beat of silence (marked [09:26]) after is probably a visual reaction that plays well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She didn't know any moves, you know? I tried to teach her, but she wouldn't listen to any of my commands.

jokes.text: Tammy ends the conversation by saying 'I have to take a shit' — mirroring Dee's earlier excuse
jokes.setup: Dee used 'taking a shit' as her excuse to maneuver earlier; now Dee's seduction has completely failed
jokes.punchline: Tammy dismisses Dee with the same line — the ultimate brushoff, mirroring Dee's own crudeness back at her
jokes.explanation: Elegant callback structure — the 'shit' running gag gets a third use here as a dismissal weapon turned on Dee. The episode has established this phrase as a comedic reset button, and Tammy using it to end Dee's pathetic pitch is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We don't have a song. How could we have a song together? We listened to no music whatsoever. The whole thing was done in silence.

jokes.text: Post-failure debrief: Dennis says he 'couldn't do it' because Trey was 'a pussy'; Dee says Tammy was 'all over her' but she found it 'boring'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee both failed at seducing Trey and Tammy respectively
jokes.punchline: They each reframe their failure as a choice — Dennis because Trey is a 'pussy'; Dee because she found it 'boring' — when clearly neither was seduced at all
jokes.explanation: The mutual-delusion beat is on-brand for both characters. Neither can admit rejection so they both invent narratives where they were the ones choosing not to follow through. Classic Sunny self-protection comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I think the fact that she was 19 is actually the reason why Trey and Tammy didn't want their son dating her. Because she was robbing the cradle. You know?

jokes.text: 'Teen drama's forged in lust. Adult drama's forged in sadness.' / 'So sad. He was folding the laundry.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are philosophizing about why teen drama is exciting and adult drama is boring
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the pseudo-profound thesis ('forged in sadness'), then immediately applies it to Trey folding laundry as the saddest possible example
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable exchanges. 'Teen drama's forged in lust, adult drama's forged in sadness' is genuinely well-written — it's funny but also kind of true, which is the best Sunny writing. The immediate bathos of 'He was folding the laundry' perfectly grounds the thesis in the mundane tragedy of Trey's life.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I told you we had international dealings. You know what I mean? Africa is a big market for us, you know?

jokes.text: Dennis and Dee agree Trey is a 'pussy' for doing chores — 'She should be doing that. Of course, she should.'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are recapping how domestic Trey is
jokes.punchline: Their shared conviction that Tammy 'should' be doing the domestic labor — with zero self-awareness that Dennis and Dee themselves are both lazy and useless
jokes.explanation: Functional but not exceptional. The irony of Dennis and Dee judging anyone's domestic arrangement is there, but the joke doesn't quite land as sharply as the laundry lines around it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank always said he wanted his dick and his heart to explode at the same time.

jokes.text: "She should be doing that." / "Of course, she should." (About Tammy not doing laundry)
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are appalled that Trey does all the domestic work
jokes.punchline: Their shared conviction that Tammy 'should be doing that' — said by a woman who presumably does no domestic labor — is unreflective, hypocritical, and very them
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat about their retrograde assumptions. Gets the point across efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: If he did, he did it hard as a rock.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie debate why soap operas are called soap operas: 'No soap involved. And no singing. Nothing operatic about it.'
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie not to be melodramatic; Charlie asks why they call them soap operas
jokes.punchline: The genuine philosophical tangent about soap opera etymology — 'nothing operatic about it' — delivered with complete earnestness by two men investigating a disappearance
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac/Charlie tangent energy. The timing — during what should be a serious investigation — and Charlie's completely sincere curiosity make it work. The logic ('no soap involved') is funny because it's not wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Trey Jr.
dialogue.line: She said when she was in high school, you were 40.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I was 30.

dialogue.speaker: Trey Jr.
dialogue.line: What's the difference?

jokes.text: Mac describes wanting 'rising tension to make the comedy... or tragedy... feel more satisfying'
jokes.setup: Mac is advising Charlie on what kind of story Frank's disappearance should be
jokes.punchline: Mac is literally giving notes on the episode's own narrative structure, mid-episode
jokes.explanation: The meta-commentary continues — Mac is essentially a TV critic commenting on the episode he's in. 'The comedy... or tragedy' hedge is funny because he's not sure which genre they're in, which is true of the show generally.

dialogue.line: She said when she was in high school, you were 40.

jokes.text: Mac describes Frank finding a 'bullet in his head and a suicide note' as potentially having 'an overall poetic sense of completion to his inevitable story arc'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to convince Charlie that Frank's death could be narratively satisfying
jokes.punchline: Mac applies TV-critic language ('story arc,' 'poetic sense of completion') to his friend potentially being dead — with no emotional response whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny — Mac's detachment from Frank's potential death, filtered entirely through narrative theory, is a great character beat. 'Historically terrible life choices' as a euphemism for Frank's entire existence is well-put. Charlie's immediate 'That's not gonna work for me at all, man' is the right pushback.

dialogue.speaker: News Reporter
dialogue.line: Fortunately, the teens survived the crash, although both sustained injuries, and will be likely severely disfigured.

jokes.text: Cricket appears under the bridge with dreadlocks, speaking in an affected Black vernacular — the gang immediately calls this out as 'a very dangerous line'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie find Cricket under the bridge; he's taken on a new persona with dreadlocks and an affected accent
jokes.punchline: The show immediately has the characters call out that this is 'giving the ick' and they're 'dancing around a very dangerous line' — the meta-commentary on the bit IS the bit
jokes.explanation: Smart, risky meta-joke — the show has Cricket doing a problematic bit and immediately has Mac and Charlie break to essentially say 'we know, we know, we're not supposed to do this.' 'We're past it as a society' is a funny line. The self-awareness is the defense and the joke simultaneously. Whether it fully works is debatable, but the craft in how they handle it (calling it out in-scene) is high.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, I could definitely kick his ass now, right? He's all jacked up.

jokes.text: Cricket: 'If this got something to do with that john who got his dick bit off, I don't know shit... I don't know where the dick is, okay?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are questioning Cricket about Frank's whereabouts; Cricket becomes defensive
jokes.punchline: Cricket preemptively denies involvement in an entirely separate crime — a john who had his dick bitten off — which raises far more questions than the Frank mystery
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Cricket joke. The genius is that this unprompted confession/denial is exactly what someone would say if guilty. 'I don't know where the dick is, okay?' is immediately one of the best lines of the episode — it's specific, escalating, and completely in keeping with Cricket's established life of degradation. Cricket's history of prostitution-adjacent crimes makes this feel earned rather than random. Very high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know, if they're just, like, mangled and stuff, then I think it's nothing. It's not anything. Yeah, m-maybe a horror film?

jokes.text: 'Who's they?' — Mac and Charlie's simultaneous question about who has the dick
jokes.setup: Cricket says 'they take the dick and I don't know what they do with it'
jokes.punchline: Both Mac and Charlie immediately focus on 'who's they' — perfectly reasonable follow-up that Cricket refuses to answer
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the shared focus on 'who's they' is the right reaction and extends the joke. Cricket's refusal to explain makes it funnier. Part of the extended dick-bite escalation.

dialogue.speaker: News Reporter
dialogue.line: Frank's Global Youth Foundation brings joy to needy children.

jokes.text: Cricket has a Frank Reynolds NDA: 'This cricket ain't chirping.'
jokes.setup: Cricket claims he can't reveal information about Frank because of an NDA
jokes.punchline: 'This cricket ain't chirping' — a self-referential pun on his own name, delivered in his affected voice
jokes.explanation: Cricket using his own name as a pun in the context of an NDA ('not chirping' = not talking) is a nicely economical joke. The delivery timing matters — it lands as a moment of self-satisfaction from Cricket.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, that's what you call a plot twist.

jokes.text: Mac's reaction to the NDA: 'That's good, that brings us right back around to a mystery.' / 'How is that good, dude?'
jokes.setup: Cricket reveals Frank made him sign an NDA, blocking information
jokes.punchline: Mac's immediate genre-classification of this development ('it means there's a paper trail') frames it as exciting plot advancement — Charlie's exasperated 'how is that good, dude?' is the straight-man response
jokes.explanation: Continuation of the meta-genre-commentary joke. Mac treating every obstacle as a narrative opportunity is consistent and funny, but slightly less fresh than its earlier iterations.

jokes.text: Cricket threatens to 'kick the shit out' of Mac for stepping to him — 'That's how he bit the dick off'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to pressure Cricket; Cricket gets aggressive
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate connection of Cricket's threatening stance to the dick-biting incident — 'That's how he bit the dick off' — implies Cricket escalates to biting dicks when confronted
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. The logic — that Cricket's threatening energy is exactly what preceded the dick-biting — is both funny and weirdly coherent. 'That's how he bit the dick off' as a warning about escalation is immediately quotable. High character integration: only Cricket's specific history makes this joke possible.

jokes.text: Cricket's NDA names the lawyer as 'Jack Kelly, attorney at lawyering'
jokes.setup: Mac reads the NDA looking for useful information; finds the lawyer's name
jokes.punchline: 'Jack Kelly, attorney at lawyering' — Uncle Jack's self-written professional title is hilariously unqualified
jokes.explanation: 'Attorney at lawyering' is a perfect recurring character joke — Uncle Jack's perpetual near-miss on professional legitimacy, here crystallized in his inability to write his own title correctly. The reveal lands as both a plot twist and a great character joke. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Uncle Jack: 'Okay, you sure this wouldn't be better to handle at my office?' / 'You have an office?'
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack appears as Frank's lawyer
jokes.punchline: His suggestion of handling business 'at my office' is immediately questioned — implying he doesn't have one
jokes.explanation: Classic Uncle Jack joke — his pretense of professionalism immediately undercut. 'That in itself is a mysterious twist' from Mac is a good meta-commentary kicker.

jokes.text: Uncle Jack's 'office' is revealed to be Mac's mom's basement with a filing cabinet
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack claims to have an office
jokes.punchline: Mac flatly reveals it's his mom's basement — a filing cabinet and a computer
jokes.explanation: Good deflation of Uncle Jack's self-importance. 'You have a filing cabinet until the FBI comes' is a great bonus line that implies Jack's entire legal 'practice' is under federal investigation.

jokes.text: 'You have a filing cabinet until the FBI comes.'
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack claims to have a proper office setup (filing cabinet and computer)
jokes.punchline: Mac casually notes the FBI will eventually take even that — implying Jack is definitely committing crimes with whatever he's filing
jokes.explanation: Very economical dark joke — in nine words, Mac implies Jack is a criminal, incompetent, and operating on borrowed time. The casual delivery is essential. High quotability as a standalone line.

jokes.text: Frank has listed Charlie as 'president of Frank's foundation' — Mac is not listed anywhere
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack can only share info with whoever Frank designated; it turns out to be Charlie
jokes.punchline: Mac is not listed anywhere in Frank's affairs — despite Frank being his friend — and the humiliation is delivered with bureaucratic indifference
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Mac's exclusion from Frank's foundation mirrors his general status in the group (always slightly outside the core Frank/Charlie bond). 'I'm not seeing you listed anywhere in here' as a bureaucratic dismissal is funny. Sets up Charlie's immediate power trip.

jokes.text: Charlie immediately goes on a power trip about being 'president' — 'These are big decisions that are kind of over your head, man'
jokes.setup: Charlie just learned he's president of Frank's foundation — a role he knows nothing about
jokes.punchline: He immediately lords it over Mac with 'big decisions that are kind of over your head, man' — delivered with zero awareness that he has even less idea what's happening
jokes.explanation: Excellent Charlie moment — his immediate pivot from confused to imperious is perfect. 'Kind of over your head, man' from arguably the least qualified person in the room is great irony. High character integration: Charlie's combination of incompetence and sudden grandiosity is very specific to him.

jokes.text: "There's a lot to think about now that I'm president. You know what I mean? I got to find Frank. I got to find out what I'm president of."
jokes.setup: Charlie is revealed to be president of Frank's foundation
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response is to treat the presidency with great seriousness while admitting he has no idea what the foundation does
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie logic. He immediately upgrades his self-importance based on a title he doesn't understand for an organization he can't describe. 'These are big decisions that are kind of over your head, man' — said to Dennis — is especially good.

jokes.text: Mac snatches the address from Uncle Jack — 'I didn't sign off on that maneuver'
jokes.setup: Uncle Jack says he'll pass the info to Charlie; Mac needs the address for his job
jokes.punchline: Mac physically takes the information; Charlie's protest is 'I didn't sign off on that maneuver' — treating a simple paper-grab as a formal procedural violation
jokes.explanation: 'I didn't sign off on that maneuver' is funny bureaucratic language applied to a physical scuffle. Charlie's new presidential authority immediately being tested and his impotent protest is good character work.

jokes.text: The genre shifts to 'political thriller' — Mac: 'Ah. I like those. Needs a chase scene. You want to chase me around the apartment?'
jokes.setup: Mac declares their story has 'transitioned into a bit of a political thriller'
jokes.punchline: His immediate solution is to have a chase scene — specifically, Uncle Jack chasing him around the apartment — as if adding genre conventions manually will improve the plot
jokes.explanation: Great escalation of the meta-genre joke — Mac not just classifying the story but trying to actively direct it by suggesting a chase scene with Uncle Jack. 'We're not gonna do that with you, Uncle Jack' is the right deflation. The image of Uncle Jack chasing Mac around a basement apartment is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Dennis reveals he 'banged' Kerry Bitaberry — Trey Jr.'s prom date — using the excuse that Trey Jr. cheated on her
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are debriefing; Dennis claims a win
jokes.punchline: Dennis pivoted from trying to seduce Tammy to seducing Trey Jr.'s prom date — a 19-year-old — through manipulation, then complains she 'didn't know any moves'
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis escalation — his failure with Tammy simply redirected him to a more vulnerable target, whom he then manipulated. The reveal is well-paced. The horror of this is part of the joke.

jokes.text: Dennis complains Kerry 'didn't know any moves' and 'wouldn't listen to any of my commands'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining why sleeping with Kerry Bitaberry was 'kind of gross'
jokes.punchline: His complaints are entirely about her performance — she didn't follow 'commands' — revealing his sexual worldview as one where he issues orders to partners
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific Dennis joke — the word 'commands' is perfect, implying a whole disturbing dynamic. This is Dennis's psychology distilled: he has 'commands' he issues to sexual partners, and his complaint is non-compliance. High character integration.

jokes.text: Kerry made Dennis a playlist — 'We don't have a song. How could we have a song together? We listened to no music whatsoever. The whole thing was done in silence.'
jokes.setup: Kerry is blowing up Dennis's phone after their encounter
jokes.punchline: 'The whole thing was done in silence. Except for the noises that I was making.' — the horror of Dennis's silent, command-based sexual encounter is revealed by detail
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dennis joke with perfect escalation. The sequence: 'we don't have a song' → 'we listened to no music' → 'the whole thing was done in silence' → 'except for the noises I was making.' Each step is funnier and more disturbing. 'The noises I was making' is a great Sunny-style horror-comedy button. High quotability and rewatch value.

jokes.text: Dee: 'The fact that she's a child.' Dennis: 'No, she's not a child. She's 19 years old. I checked.'
jokes.setup: Dee is disgusted; Dennis asks what's grossing her out
jokes.punchline: 'I checked' — the two most damning words possible, implying Dennis verified her age specifically to establish legality, which is exactly what a predator would do
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dennis lines in the episode. 'I checked' in this context implies the entire horrifying backstory: Dennis specifically verified her age, the implication being he would have done it anyway and wanted legal cover. Two words that do as much characterization as a monologue. Economically near-perfect. Comparable in compression to the best Sunny character-reveal jokes.

jokes.text: Kerry Bitaberry's 'inability to satisfy a lover' is framed as 'the only crime here'
jokes.setup: Dee calls Dennis sleeping with a 19-year-old 'a crime'
jokes.punchline: Dennis inverts this — the only crime is Kerry's insufficient technique, not any of Dennis's behavior
jokes.explanation: Dennis's moral inversion — where the crime is not what he did but that his partner was inadequate — is a perfect character beat. The confidence of 'Kerry Bitaberry's inability to satisfy a lover' as a formal charge is funny.

jokes.text: 'No, she's not a child. What're you talking about? She's 19 years old. I checked.'
jokes.setup: Dee calls Kerry Bitaberry 'a child.' Dennis defends himself.
jokes.punchline: 'I checked.' — The word 'checked' implies verification done in advance, which raises more questions than it answers about Dennis's process.
jokes.explanation: 'I checked' is a devastating two-word callback to Dennis's established predator behavior. It implies a systematic verification process, which is somehow worse than not checking. Perfectly economical. Absolutely Dennis. High quotability — it's the kind of line that lands harder every time you think about what it implies.

jokes.text: Dennis's argument: Kerry was 'robbing the cradle' because she's 19 and dating a teenage Trey Jr.
jokes.setup: Dennis is defending why Trey and Tammy didn't want Kerry dating their son
jokes.punchline: He argues Kerry (19) was 'robbing the cradle' with a teenage Trey Jr. — while Dennis himself just slept with Kerry — with no self-awareness whatsoever
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis self-delusion — he applies 'robbing the cradle' to a 19-year-old dating a teenager while being a middle-aged man who just slept with that 19-year-old. The complete absence of self-awareness is the joke, and it's textbook Dennis. 'Okay. All right.' from Dee, who clearly can't even begin to address this, is the right non-response.

jokes.text: Dee announces she needs to go 'bang Trey Jr.' — 'Because we're doing a thing, and I got to win'
jokes.setup: Dennis has successfully slept with Kerry; Dee hasn't slept with anyone yet
jokes.punchline: Dee's motivation is purely competitive — she's going to sleep with a teenager because she needs to win whatever competition she's decided they're in
jokes.explanation: Dee's decision to pursue a teenager purely out of competition with Dennis is exactly her character. 'I got to win' as the entire justification is funny in its simplicity. Dennis's 'Hmm. All right.' — complete acceptance — is the right beat.

jokes.text: The storage unit address code is '6969' — 'Every time.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie arrive at Frank's storage unit and need the code
jokes.punchline: '6969. Every time.' — implying Frank always uses this code, which is consistent with Frank's established character
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient Frank-character joke. 'Every time' implies this is established Frank behavior, which is funnier than it being a one-off. Well-economized — two words do the character work.

jokes.text: Charlie declares himself president of an international toy-trading foundation: 'Africa is a big market for us, you know? We do a lot of trading in the toy sector.'
jokes.setup: The storage unit contains boxes labeled 'Toys for the foundation. Ship to Africa.'
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately claims ownership of these international operations with fake authority — 'Don't even ask too many questions about it' — while clearly having no idea what any of this is
jokes.explanation: Charlie's instant adoption of presidential authority over Frank's mysterious operation — with zero information — is great. 'Don't ask too many questions about it' implies both that it's shady and that Charlie has no answers. The power-trip escalation from the earlier foundation reveal continues well.

jokes.text: Charlie insisting Frank has 'international dealings' because the storage unit has boxes labeled 'Ship to Africa.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie find a storage unit full of boxes labeled 'Toys for the foundation. Ship to Africa.'
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately claims this as evidence that he, as Foundation President, oversees 'international dealings' — 'Africa is a big market for us, you know? We do a lot of... trading in the toy sector.'
jokes.explanation: Charlie's instant expansion of his presidential authority is a good bit. His vague hand-waving about 'trading in the toy sector' and warning Mac not to 'pry' into international business he literally just discovered is well-played.

jokes.text: 'Oh, these are dick pills, man.' — Mac's flat discovery of Rhino dick pills in the storage unit
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are exploring the storage unit filled with mysterious boxes, building toward some kind of dramatic revelation
jokes.punchline: The pivot from mysterious toys/foundation to 'dick pills' — delivered with zero drama — completely deflates the thriller atmosphere they've been cultivating
jokes.explanation: Perfect genre-deflation joke — Mac's flat 'oh, these are dick pills, man' punctures any thriller tension they've been building. The deadpan delivery is essential. 'Jesus. All right, well, it took a sexual turn. That's kind of interesting.' from Charlie treats this as a mere narrative beat, which is funny.

jokes.text: Frank's taped message: 'I lost one to racial injustice. Another one OD'd. Lost a wife to a botched neck job.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie find a VHS tape they expect to be Frank naked; instead it's a heartfelt message about love
jokes.punchline: Frank's list of lost loves is a rapid-fire escalation of tragedy, each more absurd than the last — 'botched neck job' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: Frank's earnest tragedy speech is elevated by the specificity and escalation of losses: racial injustice → OD → botched neck job. Each is more Frank-specific than the last. 'That's a whole other story' on the neck job is a funny throwaway that implies Frank could go on. The genuine pathos competing with the absurdity is classic Sunny.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie's realization: Frank taped over Highlander episodes and ran out of tape
jokes.setup: Frank's heartfelt tape appears to end abruptly
jokes.punchline: He taped over old Highlander VHS tapes and simply ran out of tape — the technical failure undermines the emotional moment
jokes.explanation: Good Frank detail — the VHS medium (antique), the Highlander choice (Frank's taste), and 'he always forgets where the tape ends' all combine into a compact character portrait. The technical failure as emotional punchline is a good structural choice.

jokes.text: 'Frank always said he wanted his dick and his heart to explode at the same time.' / 'If he did, he did it hard as a rock.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie realize the empty dick pill bottles suggest Frank overdosed on sexual enhancement drugs
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals Frank's stated ideal death; Mac's response — 'he did it hard as a rock' — is both a literal description and an inadvertent tribute
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best Frank jokes in the series. 'He wanted his dick and his heart to explode at the same time' is perfectly Frank — hedonistic, absurd, oddly poetic. Mac's 'If he did, he did it hard as a rock' is a flawless double entendre that works as both a eulogy and a crude joke. The structure is impeccable: setup (Frank's stated wish) → evidence (empty pill bottles) → Charlie's revelation → Mac's perfect button. Comparable to the vasectomy anchor example in character specificity and shock-to-laugh ratio.

jokes.text: "Frank always said he wanted his dick and his heart to explode at the same time." / "Dude, did he kill himself?" / "If he did, he did it hard as a rock."
jokes.setup: They find all the dick pills are empty and worry Frank has overdosed on them
jokes.punchline: Mac's conclusion: if Frank died from too many dick pills, 'he did it hard as a rock' — which is both a crude joke and a genuine Frank eulogy
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and arguably the season. 'He did it hard as a rock' works on every level: (1) it's a perfect dark joke about Frank's brand, (2) it's unexpectedly moving as a final word on Frank's character, (3) the economy is flawless — six words do enormous emotional and comedic work. The setup ('Frank always said he wanted his dick and his heart to explode at the same time') is itself a great character-defining line. This is comfortably in 8+ territory.

jokes.text: Dee arrives at Trey Jr.'s door and immediately recoils: 'Jesus Christ. You are a boy.'
jokes.setup: Dee has decided to sleep with Trey Jr. to compete with Dennis
jokes.punchline: In person, Trey Jr. is clearly a child — 'You are a boy' — and Dee's horror is immediate
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — Dee's confidence is immediately demolished upon seeing him in person. 'You are a boy' as a reaction is both funny and plays on Dee's earlier proclamation of needing to 'win.' The horror of the situation is the joke.

jokes.text: Dee tries to pivot to seduction anyway: 'Let's just power through and get to the hot part, right? So, sex. Sex...'
jokes.setup: Dee has just said 'you are a boy' but hasn't left
jokes.punchline: She tries to push through her own moral hesitation with 'let's just power through and get to the hot part' — framing statutory near-miss as a scheduling inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Dee's desperate 'power through' energy is very funny and characteristic — she can see the problem clearly and chooses to try to ignore it. 'So, sex. Sex...' as a seduction line is brilliantly bad. The cringe is carefully calibrated.

jokes.text: Trey Jr.: 'The kids at my school have been sleeping with each other for a decade.'
jokes.setup: Dee nervously offers that sex might be 'a little nerve-racking' for an inexperienced young man
jokes.punchline: He corrects her — his school has been sexually active 'for a decade' — implying they started very young, which makes this worse
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke — Dee's attempt to seem experienced and worldly is immediately undercut by the teen who's clearly more experienced than she expected. 'For a decade' implies they started around age 8, which is a horrifying implication that the show hangs a lantern on.

jokes.text: Trey Jr. says Dee is barely older than his grandmother
jokes.setup: Dee has arrived trying to seduce Trey Jr., presenting herself as an older, worldly woman
jokes.punchline: 'My granny isn't that much older than you.' — Dee's attempt to be seductively mature is countered by being compared to a grandmother
jokes.explanation: Good Dee humiliation joke — the reversal of power (the supposed seductress being compared to a grandmother by her target) is well-executed. Mirrors the earlier 'grandpa' insult to Dennis, completing a symmetry.

jokes.text: Dee: 'I went to high school with your mom.' Trey Jr.: 'She said when she was in high school, you were 40.' Dee: 'I was 30!' Trey Jr.: 'What's the difference?' Dee: 'Ten years! Ten years is the diff—'
jokes.setup: Dee invokes her high school connection to Tammy to establish rapport
jokes.punchline: Tammy apparently told her son Dee was 40 in high school; Dee's indignant 'I was 30!' corrects the wrong insult while confirming she was an adult in high school with teenagers
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. Tammy told her son Dee was 40 in high school (exaggerated), Dee corrects to 30 — which is exactly what Dennis corrected earlier — and Trey Jr.'s 'What's the difference?' captures the teen's correct assessment: 30 and 40 are both old to be in high school with teenagers. Dee's explosive '10 years!' only digs her hole deeper. The structure (Dee invoking high school as a credential → being exposed by that credential) is perfect. Mirrors joke #10 with Dee in the Dennis role.

jokes.text: Dee tells Trey Jr. that Dennis slept with his prom date to provoke jealousy: 'Does that make you sad? Do you want to suck your thumb, little boy?'
jokes.setup: Dee's seduction attempt has completely collapsed; she pivots to psychological manipulation
jokes.punchline: 'Do you want to suck your thumb, little boy?' — Dee's attempt at power and seduction has devolved into taunting a teenager
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dee collapse — from attempted seducer to taunting a teenager about his prom date. 'Do you want to suck your thumb, little boy?' is the kind of line that only Dee would think is effective. The pivot from seduction to cruelty as a power move is exactly her character.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Of course it was [a win/lose thing], all right, but to be very clear — the kid wanted to, I just, I'm not a criminal.'
jokes.setup: Dee returns and says Dennis 'wins'; Dennis claims it 'wasn't really a win/lose thing'
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts himself: 'Of course it was' — then pivots to 'I'm not a criminal' as his defense, which raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis self-contradiction — the false modesty immediately dropped to reveal the competitive reality, then the defensive 'I'm not a criminal' implying that's exactly the standard he's measuring himself against.

jokes.text: News broadcast: Trey Jr. and Kerry Bitaberry drove off the Strawberry Mansion Bridge in a suicide attempt — both survived but are 'severely disfigured'
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee are debriefing about their failed/successful seductions
jokes.punchline: The local news announces that the two teenagers — whose romantic drama Dennis and Dee directly caused — attempted suicide and survived but are now 'severely disfigured'
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny consequence delivery — the gang's actions have caused a Romeo-and-Juliet-style tragedy, but they survived to be disfigured rather than dying romantically. The 'severely disfigured' detail is funnier than death would be. The juxtaposition of the mundane newscast tone against the horror of the content is well-executed.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Well, I could definitely kick his ass now, right? He's all jacked up.'
jokes.setup: News reports that Trey Jr. is severely injured from driving off a bridge
jokes.punchline: Dennis's first reaction is that this is good news — he can now beat up Trey Jr. in a fight because the teen is compromised
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis reaction — his concern is not for the teenager he partially drove to suicide but for his own physical advantage in a pending fight. 'He's all jacked up' as a tactical assessment of an injured teen is very Dennis. 'You're not gonna make me feel bad about this, okay? I don't feel bad.' — the defensive preemptive strike on guilt is excellent.

jokes.text: 'You're not gonna make me feel bad about this, okay? I don't feel bad... don't feel anything.'
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts to the news of teen suicide attempt caused by Dennis's actions
jokes.punchline: Dennis's layered non-guilt: 'I don't feel bad' escalating to 'don't feel anything' — the affectless sociopathy played as a brag
jokes.explanation: Dennis's emotional vacancy as a running character trait gets a good articulation here. 'Don't feel anything' as a final, calm statement — not defensive, just factual — is very Dennis. Character integration is high.

jokes.text: Mac's genre analysis of the teen bridge incident: 'it's really only a tragedy if they die. If they're just, like, mangled and stuff, then I think it's nothing. It's not anything. Maybe a horror film?'
jokes.setup: Frank's situation is being discussed alongside the teen bridge incident.
jokes.punchline: Mac applies his genre taxonomy to real tragedy: not a tragedy if they're 'just mangled' — maybe a horror film. His aesthetic framework has completely replaced his moral one.
jokes.explanation: Mac's storytelling-theory obsession reaches its darkest payoff here. His conclusion that disfigured-but-alive is 'nothing... maybe a horror film' is both a great punchline and a devastating character moment. The genre framework has become genuinely morally bankrupt.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Speaking of suicide, Dennis almost killed a couple of teenagers.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have just announced Frank's suicide attempt; conversation shifts
jokes.punchline: Dennis pivots from Frank's crisis to his own news with 'speaking of suicide' — treating teen suicide and an old man's dick-pill overdose as equivalent conversation topics to segue between
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Speaking of suicide' as a casual transition between Frank's overdose and Dennis's teen-driving-off-a-bridge is a masterclass in dark comedy economy. The connection is tangential enough to be absurd while also being technically valid.

jokes.text: Mac's genre re-classification: 'Maybe teen drama does have some weight to it 'cause that's, like, a tragedy.' Dennis: 'Well, I mean, it's really only a tragedy if they die. If they're just mangled... then I think it's nothing.'
jokes.setup: Mac is reconsidering his dismissal of teen drama given the actual teen tragedy that's unfolded
jokes.punchline: Dennis applies a formal tragedy definition — 'only a tragedy if they die' — to dismiss moral concern about two teenagers he drove to attempted suicide
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. Dennis applying Aristotelian tragedy criteria to determine his own moral culpability — 'it's only a tragedy if they die; if they're just mangled, it's nothing' — is exceptional. It's the meta-genre commentary, the character's sociopathy, and the dark comedy all converging. 'Maybe a horror film?' as the alternative genre is a perfect button. High structure, very high character integration, and the economy of 'it's nothing' as the final word on two disfigured teenagers is devastating and funny.

jokes.text: Frank is on TV as 'The Golden Bachelor' — 'Frank Reynolds is looking for love. Frank's Global Youth Foundation brings joy to needy children.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have been investigating Frank's mysterious disappearance, convinced he's suicided by dick-pill overdose
jokes.punchline: Frank is on a Bachelor-style dating show for older adults — the 'global youth foundation' (suspicious toy shipments to Africa) is now being described on TV as benevolent charity
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-closing twist that retroactively recontextualizes everything. Frank's mysterious VHS message about love, the 'Global Youth Foundation' shipping toys to Africa, and the dick pills all click into place: he's going on a reality dating show and has been orchestrating his entrance as a 'philanthropist.' The twist is both surprising and inevitable. 'Well, that's what you call a plot twist' is Mac's perfect button on the meta-genre arc. Mac being satisfied by genre resolution is consistent with his entire character through the episode.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Well, that's what you call a plot twist.' — on Frank being The Golden Bachelor
jokes.setup: Frank's appearance on The Golden Bachelor resolves the episode's mystery
jokes.punchline: Mac closes the loop on the episode's genre commentary — it was always going to be a 'plot twist,' and he's satisfied
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the episode's sustained meta-joke. Mac's satisfaction in finally having his narrative category confirmed — it was indeed a plot twist — closes the circle on a clever structural device. Five words that pay off 20 minutes of genre commentary.

tmdb_overview: When Tammy and Trey, now in their 40s, show up to remove their teenage son from Paddy's, Dennis and Dee attempt to reconnect with their former prom dates. Frank's sudden disappearance sends Mac and Charlie on a mission to track down his whereabouts.
